conditions: No weapon, armour or kit line may carry a flat damage bonus or any gear-sourced additive; the largest value that keeps every tier of a row inside the ladder is zero.

Weapon identity is expressed only through the Disciplines-Required column, the Properties column and the card-visible Kit tags; the weapon catalogue may remain as colour and no numeric column may be added to it.

The weapon table's requirement column is made the single live gate: the class-kit prerequisite waiver is deleted or restated as a pointer, and the nine class Starting Kit lines are rewritten in the category form the Class Recommendations surface already uses, so no printed kit demands a rank its class cannot grant.

Every weapon recipe must be made distinct and co-monotone with what the weapon can do, so that no cheaper armament out-permits a costlier one; the eight strict dominations found across the card corpus are removed by price, not by a number.

A damage-type or other multiplier surface on hero weapons ships only together with the printed gate that prevents it from lifting a row above the next band; until that gate exists, type is not an identity channel.
Any Discipline used as a weapon gate must carry card coverage at every rank it prices; a gate that opens no card is repaired by authoring cards or by lowering the price, not left standing.
Additions to the property vocabulary are priced on the same rate standard as the fix itself, and properties that no printed rule reads are dropped rather than promoted.
point_of_contention: On which surface must weapon identity be carried: in the permission layer already printed for weapons (the Discipline recipe in the requirement column, the property list, and the tags a card header can read), or in a damage magnitude attached to the weapon itself, and may a weapon carry any flat damage number at all?
reasoning: Seven speakers filed on this topic and six of the seven ended in support; the one finding standing against the proposition, Speaker B's round-two entry, attacks a cost estimate and one weapon-side multiplier rather than defending a weapon magnitude, and Speaker B's other round-two finding backs the same permission model. The arithmetic behind the ban on addition converges from two independent directions. Speaker B tested the additive channel directly and could not break substitution: a one-point gear bonus still leaves three distinct tiers, a two-point bonus delivers the Master band to an Adept character a tier early, a three-point bonus inverts the ladder, and the attribute-scaled spine keeps only one point of headroom in total. Speaker B also produced the asymmetry that settles it: kit gear is re-specified free at every town while card values are bought with points, so a bonus attached to gear costs less than the card figure it undercuts, which makes it a breach of the level-gate rule rather than a way around it. Speaker F reached the same ceiling from the printed bands alone and supplied the reason: the tightest step in the ladder is a single point and a constant carries no level, whereas a weapon written as a recipe inherits the tier's price, its gate and its row, so nothing can arrive early. Speaker A's round-two entry also asserts no magnitude and offers damage type as the empty identity slot, but Speaker B's red team showed that the doubling already printed in the corpus turns a first-tier row into figures that match the next band's middle and exceed its top; Speaker A never answered that, so type cannot serve as an identity channel until a gate on it is printed. On location, Speaker D showed that the book runs two permission models over the same gear and that the class kits are the seam where they collide, leaving the requirement column unenforced; Speaker D's reconciliation closes it with three rule lines, one pointer and nine kit lines, re-keying no cards and adding no tags. Speaker B's repricing spec removes eight strict dominations by making each recipe distinct and charging each capability, still without a number on a weapon. Speaker G's worked heroes show the per-turn choice coming from properties rather than recipes, and expose a Discipline that buys nothing at rank one or three, so a recipe without card coverage is a gate in form only. On size, Speaker E measured that keeping the catalogue as colour costs no folio and no table-of-contents renumbering, and Speaker C found only three of the seven properties read by any rule outside their own definition; against that, Speaker B priced Speaker A's seven-property platform at roughly two hundred further gated cards on Speaker A's own parity standard, while Speaker C priced a trimmed five-tag version at about ten gate sites. The architecture is therefore common ground; only its size is contested, and the smallest compliant version is the one the conditions require.
ruling: Rule for the permission layer: a weapon's identity is carried only by what it permits, never by magnitude. The identity surfaces are the Discipline recipe in the weapon table's requirement column, the weapon's property set, and the tags a card header can read; a flat damage number, tier bump or better-weapon ladder printed on a weapon row is out of bounds, because the largest gear-sourced value that leaves the damage ladder intact is zero. The requirement column is the single live gate: the class-kit prerequisite waiver is deleted or narrowed to a pointer rather than left standing beside it, and recipes are to be repaired by price and card coverage rather than by a number. A multiplier surface on hero-side weapons, damage type included, may not ship unless the same change prints the gate that stops it lifting a row above the next band. Round 2 is to be built inside this boundary.
